The following rules apply to the placement of stress on the word level. 1. The first syllable of a word which contains /a/ is stressed. 2. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress: the syllable containing /a/ is stressed; otherwise the first syllable. The conditioning factor is vowel quality (the low vowel /a/ among /i, a, o, u/ in this dialect), not syllable structure; no tone, no length. The one-sentence 'either.. or' does not say which clause wins or give stress-marked examples (the 1978 primary resolves the ordering).
new_statements.identity_note: Foreman & Marten 1978 (like the 1973 paper it revises) states in its introduction that 'This paper is based on the river dialect' (approx. 600 speakers on or near the Sepik River 20-30 miles upriver from Ambunti; the other dialect, approx. 400 speakers, lives north and west in the flat forest). Marten 1995 describes the Yawu dialect (population 740 in 1995; villages listed as Bur, Bwiyou, Manamei, Warsai and one more), i.e. the non-river dialect = Glottolog yawu1237. The 2004 OPD is language-level, 'Yessan-Mayo Language [YSS] (New name: Yamano)'. Both dialects are given the same stress rule.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and non-phonemic. Rule 1: the first (leftmost) syllable containing /a/ is stressed; rule 2 (elsewhere case): if the word has no /a/, the first syllable is stressed. Examples show stress skipping a non-/a/ initial syllable to land on /a/ (si'pa 'seed', wu'řamse 'tobacco', tʰɔk'naᵐbʌ 'sleeping') and initial stress in /a/-less words ('tʰetete, 'lowsi). Conditioning is vowel quality (the lowest vowel), not CVC/CVV weight: no length contrast, codas play no role ('lowsi). No tone. Two intonation contours (tentative pause rising, final pause falling) are phrase-level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned; in this 1978 revision 'sleeping' carries a single stress mark on the /a/ syllable (tʰɔk'naᵐbʌ), whereas the 1973 published version marked it twice ('tʰowk'naᵐbʌ)

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding 1973 passage and both later restatements are verbatim in held page scan/scanned at the stated locators. Deciding source is the dedicated SIL phonemic statement (1973) by the language's principal describers, with explicit rules and stress-marked examples; a 1978 revision of the same paper (SIL archives 31302, downloaded now via the Internet Archive, scanned p.25) repeats the two rules word for word with re-transcribed examples, and the 1995 and 2004 documents agree. Glottolog's bibliography contains no competing or later phonological description; the only unheld substantial work is Foreman's own 1974 grammar, available only via controlled lending, which is unlikely to change a SEGMENTAL-OTHER (leftmost /a/, else initial) coding.org full-catalog search, and the the Internet Archive
